title: Drinking Alone Under the Moon
program_note:
Drinking Alone Under the Moon, a setting of the poem with the same title by the Tang Dynasty poet Li Bai (701-762, also known as Li Po), was composed for the Bridges East and West exchange between UCLA and Beijing Capital Normal University.
The music begins with a musical depiction of the natural surroundings, including insects, birds, other wildlife, and the stars above, emphasizing the poet’s loneliness.  The poet at first uses the presence of the moon and moonlight as an excuse not to drink alone, but as the music comes to a close his appreciation of his closeness to all of nature and (especially) the heavens emerges.
The texts — the Chinese original, and an English translation, both of which are used in the music — are given below.

Drinking Alone Under the Moon

相 永 醉 醒 我 我 行 暫 影 月 對 舉 獨 花      月
期 結 後 時 舞 歌 樂 伴 徒 既 影 杯 酌 間       下      李
邈 無 各 同 影 月 須 月 隨 不 成 邀 無 一      獨      白
雲 情 分 交 零 徘 及 將 我 解 三 明 相 壺       酌
漢 遊 散 歡 亂 徊 春 影 身 飲 人 月 親 酒

A jug of wine, out among the flowers,
All alone, no friends here to drink with me,
So I invite the moon, “come spend some hours!
With you, my shadow and I will be three.”

The moon does not know much about drinking
And my shadow always mimes me, it’s true;
But I’ll be happy enough, I’m thinking,
To satisfy me until spring is through.

When I sing aloud, the moon slips and slides,
When I dance, my shadow stumbles and sways.
While still sober each happily abides,
When we’re drunk we go our separate ways.

Our friendship will outlast all earthly love;
We’ll meet again beyond the stars above.

Text by Li Bai
(Translation by David S. Lefkowitz)

David S. Lefkowitz
Los Angeles, CA
25 July, 2016
